say: Welcome back, inquirers! Today is pizza day: we share pizzas fairly, cut them in clever ways and find out what the Ancient Egyptians knew about fractions.
Notice it, test it, explain why: by the end you will solve fraction puzzles that trip up grown-ups.
Fraction Face-off! Two fractions appear. One finger if the first is bigger, two fingers if the second is bigger.

Tell your partner a reason in a whisper: same top? Close to 1? More than a whole? Try it without common denominators first, but any method is welcome. I will only ask volunteers to share, and you may pass.
3 pizzas are shared equally among 4 friends. Will each friend get more than half a pizza or less? Write your prediction before you cut anything.
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: cut every pizza into 4 equal pieces. How many pieces are there? How many does each friend get?
Too many pieces: can you cut some pizzas in halves and only one into quarters?
If a pair wants more: share 5 pizzas among 6 friends so that each friend gets just 2 pieces.

say: “3 pizzas among 4 friends. If I cut each pizza into quarters, there are 12 quarters and each friend gets 3 of them: 3/4. So 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4. The top number is what is shared, the bottom number is how many share it.”

“Now 7/12 as two different unit fractions. I try in order. 1/2: 7/12 − 6/12 = 1/12, a unit fraction, yes. 1/3: 7/12 − 4/12 = 3/12 = 1/4, yes. 1/4: what is left is 1/3, the same pair again. Once my first part is smaller than half of 7/12, the other part would be bigger, so I stop. Two ways.”

“Mei had 180 beads. She used 1/3 for a bracelet and 3/4 of the REMAINDER for a necklace. I draw a bar in 3 parts. The remainder is 2 parts, which I cut into 4 small units, so the whole bar is 6 small units. Bracelet 2, necklace 3, left 1. 6 units = 180, so 1 unit = 30. She has 30 beads left.”

do: Ask: “Is that a fraction of the whole or of the remainder?”
Ask: “How do you know you have found all the ways? When can you stop?”
Ask: “Show me your model. Are all the small units the same size?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw a bar. Cut it into the parts the first fraction tells you.”
Hint 2: “Cut the remainder again so every unit in the bar is the same size.”
Hint 3: “Take away the unit fraction and simplify. Is the top number 1?”

do: Ask: “Is that a fraction of the whole or of the remainder?”
Ask: “How do you know you have found all the ways? When can you stop?”
Ask: “Show me your model. Are all the small units the same size?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw a bar. Cut it into the parts the first fraction tells you.”
Hint 2: “Cut the remainder again so every unit in the bar is the same size.”
Hint 3: “Take away the unit fraction and simplify. Is the top number 1?”

say: “Ben says 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 because you add the tops and add the bottoms. Is he right? Use a pizza to show why.”
“In Q2, how do you know when to stop testing unit fractions?”
ask: “Ben says 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 because you add the tops and add the bottoms. Is he right? Use a pizza to show why.”

He is wrong. 1/2 of a pizza is already more than 2/5, so adding 1/3 more cannot give 2/5. Cut into sixths: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so the total is 5/6. We can only add the tops when the pieces are the same size.

say: “Today you shared pizzas, found unit fractions by testing in order, took fractions of a remainder with a model and found a pattern in fraction sums. Great inquiring!”
“Do the exit ticket on your own, then show me.”

p5l2-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Link fractions and division (3 ÷ 4 = 3/4) and divide a proper fraction by a whole number; write fractions as the sum of two different unit fractions by testing in order; solve fraction-of-a-remainder problems forwards and backwards with a bar model; and spot and explain patterns in fraction sums. Thinking strategies taught today: DRAW A MODEL (bar or pizza), TEST IN ORDER and know when to stop, find the REMAINDER first, LOOK FOR A PATTERN, and test both ways. Materials: paper circles (about 6 per child) and scissors, a paper strip for bar models, digit cards 1 to 5, mini whiteboards, workbook. Online: children cut out their paper circles before the lesson and fold or cut them on camera; the tutor shares the slides and draws the bar models live; pairs use breakout rooms for the explore and page 1. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5 (one hold-up for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6.5 to 13 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 13 to 27 (pair work 6 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 27 to 38 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 38 to 42, workbook page 1 42 to 57.5 (the questions without a star; after question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 57.5 to 61.5, short teaching before page 2 61.5 to 63, workbook page 2 63 to 71 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 71 to 74, talk time 74 to 79.5 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 79.5 to 84, reflection 84 to 86.5 (pass is always OK), stamp typed in the chat and goodbye 86.5 to 87.5, and the buffer 87.5 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation."

p5l2-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE hold-up for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone shows their paper at the same moment (own paper shown only to you as you walk round; online, all hold paper to the camera together, or show it to you only, on camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: 1/2 of a pizza each. For example cut each pizza in half: that makes 4 halves, one for each friend. Any fair cutting is fine (for example cutting each pizza into quarters and giving each friend 2 quarters).; Q2: 2/3. After the book 2/3 is left; half of 2/3 is 1/3 (lunch); 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3. The half is a half of what is LEFT, not of everything. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4.5 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: everyone holds their paper up to the camera at the same moment, or shows it to you only, on camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE hold-up for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone shows their paper at the same moment), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l2-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 9.5. Fraction Face-off. Point to one pair at a time; children show 1 or 2 fingers (nobody has to explain a finger), then pairs whisper a reason and ONLY volunteers share it; never ask a child because of the finger they showed. Answers and reasons: 3/5 is bigger than 3/7 (same top number: fewer, bigger pieces, fifths are bigger than sevenths). 6/7 is bigger than 5/6 (5/6 is 1/6 short of 1, 6/7 is only 1/7 short, and 1/7 is smaller than 1/6). 1/2 is bigger than 4/9 (4/9 is less than 4.5/9). 8/7 is bigger than 7/8 (8/7 is more than 1 and 7/8 is less than 1). Listen for the reasons that volunteers give. Praise "compare to a half" and "how far from 1" as strategies; these come back in the lesson.

p5l2-warm2.note: Minutes 9.5 to 13. Read each aloud, whiteboards up together, then click to show. 1) The top is what is shared, the bottom is how many share. 2) 4/6 + 1/6 = 5/6. 3) 20 ÷ 4 = 5, × 3 = 15. 4) 6/20 = 3/10. Ask: "Who added the bottoms in question 2?" Answers: 3/4, 5/6, 15, 3/10. If you are short of time, skip question 4.

p5l2-explore1.note: Minutes 13 to 27 (the whole explore; this slide 13 to 23). Pairs with paper circles (online: each child cuts their own). Ask them to predict first: will each friend get more or less than half a pizza? Let them find any fair way, then push for "only 2 pieces each". Pair work is at most 6 minutes. Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): 5 pizzas among 6 friends with only 2 pieces each, and the Go further what-if on the next slide. PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 6 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 23 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: 4/5, 5/6 and 6/7: the share grows each time (0.8, 0.83, 0.86). Each child is 1/5, 1/6, 1/7 short of a whole pizza, a smaller piece each time, so the shares creep up towards 1 pizza but never reach it.

p5l2-explore2.note: Minutes 23 to 27. Gather the pairs. Answers: 1) 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 of a pizza each (cut every pizza into 4: 12 quarters, 3 each). 2) Cut 2 pizzas into halves and 1 pizza into quarters: each friend gets 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, which is 2 pieces. 3) (Go further, not asked together) 5 pizzas among 6 friends with 2 pieces each: cut 3 pizzas into halves (6 halves) and 2 pizzas into thirds (6 thirds): each friend gets 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6. Say: "This is the same as writing 5/6 as a sum of two different unit fractions: 1/2 + 1/3." That is the puzzle type on the worksheet, but with different numbers. Do not give away the worksheet fractions. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): 4/5, 5/6 and 6/7: the share grows each time (0.8, 0.83, 0.86). Each child is 1/5, 1/6, 1/7 short of a whole pizza, a smaller piece each time, so the shares creep up towards 1 pizza but never reach it.

p5l2-teach1.note: Minutes 27 to 29. Teach. Draw the two pizzas cut in fifths. "Each friend takes one slice from each pizza: 1/5 + 1/5 = 2/5. So 2 ÷ 5 = 2/5." Then the second idea: a fraction divided by a whole number. Draw a bar of 5 parts with 3 shaded; cut every part in half so there are 10 small parts and 6 shaded; two friends share the 6 shaded parts: 3 each, 3/10. Say: "Dividing by 2 makes each piece twice as small, so the bottom number doubles: 3/5 ÷ 2 = 3/10." Check: 3/10 × 2 = 6/10 = 3/5. Ask: "What is 3/4 ÷ 3?" (1/4: shortcut, the top 3 can be shared in 3 groups of 1.) Children who have not met it may need the picture twice.

p5l2-try1.note: Minutes 29 to 30. Whiteboards up together, then click. a) 4 pizzas among 7: 4/7. b) 4/5 ÷ 3: cut each fifth into 3 pieces, so 4 fifths = 12 fifteenths; shared by 3 gives 4 fifteenths: 4/15. (Two items only.)

p5l2-we1.note: Minutes 30 to 32.5. Test in order, and know when to stop: today's first strategy. Click each row while children work out the subtraction first. Think-aloud: "I list the unit fractions in order, biggest first. 1/2: is it less than 7/12? Yes. 7/12 − 6/12 = 1/12, a unit fraction, so that is one way. 1/3 leaves 3/12 = 1/4, another way. 1/4 leaves 4/12 = 1/3: that is the same pair as before, so I have found them all. A unit fraction must be less than 7/12 and at least half of it (so the two parts can be different and add up): that is 1/2 and 1/3 only." Why 1/2 can be the first: 1/2 < 7/12. What about 1/1? Too big. Answer: 1/2 + 1/12 and 1/3 + 1/4. Check: 6/12 + 1/12 = 7/12 and 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

p5l2-try2.note: Minutes 32.5 to 34. Whiteboards. a) 5/6 − 1/2 = 1/3 yes; 5/6 − 1/3 = 1/2 (the same pair). b) 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4 is a unit fraction, so 1/2 + 1/4; 1/3 leaves 5/12, not a unit fraction. Ask: "How do you know when to stop?"

p5l2-we2.note: Minutes 34 to 36.5. The fraction of WHAT? Draw the bar as you go (online: use the slide, then children draw their own). Think-aloud: "A third of the beads is 1 part out of 3. The remainder is the other 2 parts. The necklace uses 3/4 of THAT, so I cut the remainder into 4 equal small units, which means I must cut the bracelet part into 2 so that every unit is the same size. Now the whole bar is 6 units." Common wrong answer: 3/4 of 180 = 135. Ask: "Is 3/4 of the whole the same as 3/4 of the remainder? Who has more, the bracelet or the necklace?" Check: bracelet 60, remainder 120, necklace 90, left 30. Total 60 + 90 + 30 = 180.

p5l2-key.note: Minutes 36.5 to 38. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Taking the second fraction of the whole amount instead of the remainder. (2) Adding tops and bottoms, 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5, or using the same unit fraction twice when the question says different. (3) Writing 3 ÷ 4 as 4/3, or multiplying instead of dividing when a fraction is shared.

p5l2-break.note: Minutes 38 to 42. 4 minutes. Call: 3/5 (up), 4/8 (out), 2/9 (crouch), 7/12 (up), 5/10 (out), 11/25 (crouch), 6/11 (up). Ask: "How did you decide without drawing? Compare the top number with half the bottom number."

p5l2-ws1.note: Minutes 42 to 57.5. Walk around. Ask "Is that a fraction of the whole or of the remainder?" before giving any help on Q2. Q3 is take-home (starred); do not wait for it. Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 2 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q1 (a) (b) and Q2 (the worked example, (a) (b)); Q3 is take-home. Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l2-ws1ans.note: Minutes 57.5 to 61.5. Click each answer after a pair explains. Q1b: 2/3 = 10/15, 3/5 = 9/15; or each child in A is 1/3 short of a pizza, in B 2/5 short. Q2: worked example 7/10 − 1/2 = 2/10 = 1/5, so 1/2 + 1/5 (the fraction wall shows 1/2 = 5/10). a) 9/20 − 1/4 = 9/20 − 5/20 = 4/20 = 1/5, so 1/4 + 1/5. b) 2/3 − 1/2 = 4/6 − 3/6 = 1/6, so 1/2 + 1/6. Think harder A1 (3/8 in two ways): 1/3 leaves 1/24; 1/4 leaves 1/8; 1/5 leaves 7/40 (not a unit fraction); after that the first part is less than half of 3/8, so stop. Q3: Ben 60, remainder 180, Ali 2/3 of 180 = 120, left 60 = 1/4 of 240.

p5l2-teachback.note: Minutes 61.5 to 63. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Start from the END of the story: what do we know? The $15 is what is left, so we know the size of one unit. Ask: "Why is the lunch exactly the same size as what is left?" (half of the remainder is spent, so half is left). Common error: working with 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6 as if both were fractions of the whole. Draw the model first, then work out one unit.

p5l2-ws2.note: Minutes 63 to 71. Children work alone on Q5 and Q4 (a); Q4 (b) (c) and Q6 are take-home (starred). Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who take the second fraction of the whole instead of the remainder. Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q5 and Q4 (a), then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 71 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l2-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71 to 74. Click after a child explains. Q4: 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3, + 1/12 = 3/4, + 1/20 = 4/5; each sum is 1 take away the next unit fraction (1 − 1/3, 1 − 1/4, 1 − 1/5), because a unit fraction minus the next unit fraction is 1 over (the number times the next number), for example 1/9 − 1/10 = 1/90. So the sum up to 1/90 (9 × 10) is 1 − 1/10 = 9/10. Q5: 10 equal units; game 4, remainder 6, book 3, left 3 units = $36, so 1 unit is $12, total $120, book $36. Q6: smallest sum: 1/3 + 2/4 = 5/6, test the other way 1/4 + 2/3 = 11/12 (bigger). Largest: 4/1 + 3/2 = 5 1/2. Closest to 1: 11/12 is 1/12 away; 5/6 is 1/6 away.

p5l2-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) 1/3 + 1/24 and 1/4 + 1/8. Test 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, … in order: 1/5 leaves 7/40, not a unit fraction; after that the first fraction would be less than half of 3/8, so stop. A2) 1/2. 2/3 was left after Ben; Ali ate 1/4 of it, so 3/4 of 2/3 = 1/2 is left. A3) 1/20 and 1/90 (the bottom numbers multiply: 4 × 5 and 9 × 10). A4) 4/6 = 2/3 of a litre.

p5l2-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 5/14. Each fraction is a difference: (1/2 − 1/3) + (1/3 − 1/4) + (1/4 − 1/5) + (1/5 − 1/6) + (1/6 − 1/7). The middle parts cancel, leaving 1/2 − 1/7 = 5/14. B2) Each child gets 5/12. Two ways: 1/3 + 1/12 (cut 4 pizzas into thirds and 1 pizza into twelfths), or 1/4 + 1/6 (cut 3 pizzas into quarters and 2 pizzas into sixths). B3) (a) 54 litres: each hour 2/3 is left, 54 → 36 → 24 → 16. (b) 2 hours: 24 litres is less than half of 54 (27), but after 1 hour 36 litres is more than half. (c) 54 − 24 = 30 litres. Make up your own (printed under Go further): Pick a fraction and write it as the sum of two different unit fractions. Challenge a partner to find your two. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l2-gofurther2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 5/14. Each fraction is a difference: (1/2 − 1/3) + (1/3 − 1/4) + (1/4 − 1/5) + (1/5 − 1/6) + (1/6 − 1/7). The middle parts cancel, leaving 1/2 − 1/7 = 5/14. B2) Each child gets 5/12. Two ways: 1/3 + 1/12 (cut 4 pizzas into thirds and 1 pizza into twelfths), or 1/4 + 1/6 (cut 3 pizzas into quarters and 2 pizzas into sixths). B3) (a) 54 litres: each hour 2/3 is left, 54 → 36 → 24 → 16. (b) 2 hours: 24 litres is less than half of 54 (27), but after 1 hour 36 litres is more than half. (c) 54 − 24 = 30 litres. Make up your own (printed under Go further): Pick a fraction and write it as the sum of two different unit fractions. Challenge a partner to find your two. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l2-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 5/14: each fraction is a difference ((1/2 − 1/3) + (1/3 − 1/4) + (1/4 − 1/5) + (1/5 − 1/6) + (1/6 − 1/7)), the middle parts cancel, leaving 1/2 − 1/7 = 5/14. 2) Each child gets 5/12. Two ways: 1/3 + 1/12 (cut 4 pizzas into thirds and 1 pizza into twelfths: 12 thirds and 12 twelfths) or 1/4 + 1/6 (cut 3 pizzas into quarters and 2 pizzas into sixths: 12 of each).

p5l2-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: E1: "Write 1/12 as a difference of two unit fractions. What happens when you add the differences one after another?" E2: "How much does each child get? Which two unit fractions add to 5/12? Try the unit fractions in order." Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l2-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. E1: show 1/6 = 1/2 − 1/3 (3/6 − 2/6 = 1/6), then ask the pattern for 1/12 (1/3 − 1/4 = 4/12 − 3/12). E2: the two ways are 1/3 + 1/12 and 1/4 + 1/6. For 1/3 + 1/12 you need 12 thirds (4 pizzas) and 12 twelfths (1 pizza); for 1/4 + 1/6 you need 12 quarters (3 pizzas) and 12 sixths (2 pizzas). Check: 4 + 1 = 5 and 3 + 2 = 5 pizzas. In the walk-through slide, 5/12 − 1/5 is not a unit fraction, and 1/5 is already less than half of 5/12, so stop (5/12 is 25/60, 1/5 is 12/60, the leftover 13/60).

p5l2-talk.note: Minutes 74 to 79.5. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: Ben is wrong. 1/2 of a pizza is already more than 2/5, so adding 1/3 more cannot give 2/5. Cut into sixths: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so the total is 5/6. We can only add the tops when the pieces are the same size. Second question only if time: "In Q2, how do you know when to stop testing unit fractions?" Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l2-exit.note: Minutes 79.5 to 84. Answers: (a) 4/5 of a pizza. (b) 20 marbles: 1/3 of 60 = 20 to Mei, 40 left, half of 40 = 20 to Ben, 20 left. Extension: write 1 as the sum of three different unit fractions (1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6, the only way).

p5l2-reflect.note: Minutes 84 to 86.5. REFLECTION, about a minute and a half. Children use the small box at the bottom of the Investigation and reflection page: Something I did well; The hardest part was; What helped me (tick boxes include "I asked for help" and "I am still stuck (my tutor will check in with me)"). Pass is always OK. Never collected in public; you may read it privately later to plan the next lesson and check in with any child who ticked still stuck in the open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, parent nearby, never a private message). Never read a child's reflection aloud. It is never collected or shown in public. You may read it privately afterwards to plan the next lesson and to check in with any child who ticked "I am still stuck", in the open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby, never a private message). Never read a child's reflection aloud; only a child who volunteers may share. Praise strategy, not speed: "Drawing the bar again when it did not work is exactly right." Then type the stamp in the chat for every child (one message) and say goodbye. If the clock is behind, the reflection becomes a one-tick version: pass or one box.
